claim: Twenty-four healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment (age ranges from 19 to 28; 17 females and 7 males, all right-handed).
source: Twenty-four healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment (age ranges from 19 to 28; 17 females and 7 males, all right-handed).
evidence: Direct statement about participant demographics in the Methods section.

claim: Two participants were excluded from the eye-tracking dataset due to the poor quality of their eye-tracking data caused by wearing glasses.
source: Two participants were excluded from the eye-tracking dataset due to the poor quality of their eye-tracking data caused by wearing glasses
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: One participant was excluded from the EEG dataset due to large number of artifacts in their EEG signal.
source: one participant was excluded from the EEG dataset due to large number of artifacts in their EEG signal.
evidence: Direct statement about data exclusion criteria.

claim: Reproduction errors were comparable across the four block types (F(3,69) = 1.378, p=0.257, η2=0.057).
source: We found comparable accuracy (reproduction errors) across the four block types (F(3,69) = 1.378, p=0.257, η2=0.057)
evidence: Statistical test results showing no significant difference in accuracy across conditions.

claim: Response times showed a significant main effect of block type (F(3,69) = 8.994, p<0.001, η2=0.281).
source: while for RTs we found a significant main effect of block type (F(3,69) = 8.994, p<0.001, η2=0.281).
evidence: Statistical test results showing significant differences in RT across conditions.

claim: There was a significant linear trend for RTs with faster responses in blocks with more reliable cues (F(1,23) = 15.304, p=0.001, η2=0.400).
source: This was corroborated by a significant linear trend (F(1,23) = 15.304, p=0.001, η2=0.400), with faster responses in blocks with more reliable cues.
evidence: Statistical test results showing a linear relationship between cue reliability and RT.

claim: Reproduction accuracy was higher (lower errors) when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item in 80% reliable-cue blocks (t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001).
source: with higher reproduction accuracy (lower errors) and faster response speed (lower RTs) when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item (80% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical comparison showing better accuracy for valid vs. invalid cues.

claim: Response times were faster when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item in 80% reliable-cue blocks (t(23) = –5.651, p<0.001).
source: with higher reproduction accuracy (lower errors) and faster response speed (lower RTs) when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item (80% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 5.357, p<0.001, RT: t(23) = –5.651, p<0.001
evidence: Statistical comparison showing faster RTs for valid vs. invalid cues.

claim: Reproduction accuracy was higher when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item in 60% reliable-cue blocks (t(23) = 3.850, p=0.012).
source: 60% reliable-cue blocks, accuracy: t(23) = 3.850, p=0.012
evidence: Statistical comparison showing better accuracy for valid vs. invalid cues.

claim: Response times were faster when the memory test probed the expected (validly cued) vs. the unexpected (invalidly cued) memory item in 60% reliable-cue blocks (t(23) = –5.286, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing faster RTs for valid vs. invalid cues.

claim: The cue-validity effect on RT was significantly larger following 80% vs 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –3.497, p=0.002).
source: For RT, this was corroborated by a significantly larger cue-validity effect following 80% vs 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –3.497, p=0.002)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing differential cue-validity effects between reliability conditions.

claim: The cue-validity effect on accuracy did not significantly differ between 80% and 60% reliable cues (t(23) = –1.533, p=0.139).
source: though for accuracy this difference did not reach significance (t(23) = –1.533, p=0.139).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference in accuracy cue-validity effects.

claim: Alpha lateralization was observed in the 100% imperative condition (cluster p<0.001).
source: In each of our four cue-reliability conditions, we found a clear alpha lateralization (cluster p: 100% imperative: p<0.001
evidence: Statistical test showing significant alpha lateralization.

claim: Alpha lateralization was observed in the 100% condition (cluster p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant alpha lateralization.

claim: Alpha lateralization was observed in the 80% condition (cluster p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant alpha lateralization.

claim: Alpha lateralization was observed in the 60% condition (cluster p=0.004).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant alpha lateralization.

claim: The spatial alpha lateralization was graded as function of cue reliability, being most pronounced for more reliable cues.
source: Consistent with prior work (Fu et al., 2022; Gould et al., 2011; Günseli et al., 2019; Haegens et al., 2012), the spatial alpha lateralization was graded as function of cue reliability, being most pronounced for more reliable cues
evidence: Observation from data analysis with reference to prior literature and Figure 2b.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cue reliability on alpha lateralization (F(3,66) = 4.711, p=0.005, η2=0.176).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of cue reliability (F(3,66) = 4.711, p=0.005, η2=0.176)
evidence: Statistical test showing effect of cue reliability on alpha lateralization.

claim: There was a significant linear trend in alpha lateralization with stronger alpha lateralization following more reliable cues (F(1,22) = 10.725, p=0.003, η2=0.328).
source: and a significant linear trend (F(1,22) = 10.725, p=0.003, η2=0.328), with stronger alpha lateralization following more reliable cues.
evidence: Statistical test showing linear relationship between cue reliability and alpha lateralization.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed in the imperative 100% condition (cluster p=0.002).
source: cluster p: 100% imperative: p=0.002
evidence: Statistical test showing significant saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed in the 100% condition (cluster p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias was observed in the 80% condition (cluster p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant saccade bias.

claim: Spatial saccade bias in the 60% condition did not reach statistical significance (cluster p=0.341).
evidence: Statistical test showing non-significant saccade bias.

claim: The difference between toward and away saccades was predominantly driven by fixational micro-saccades (<2°) rather than looking back to the original location of the items.
source: As shown in the saccade-size-over-time plots in Figure 2c, also in the current study, the difference between toward and away saccades (with red colors denoting more toward saccades) was predominantly driven by fixational saccades in the micro-saccades range (<2°).
evidence: Analysis of saccade size distribution shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cue reliability on saccade bias (F(3,63) = 11.049, p<0.001, η2=0.345).
source: The saccade bias was also graded as a function of cue reliability, as confirmed by a significant main effect of cue reliability (F(3,63) = 11.049, p<0.001, η2=0.345)
evidence: Statistical test showing effect of cue reliability on saccade bias.

claim: There was a significant linear trend in saccade bias with a more pronounced spatial saccade bias when the cue was more reliable (F(1,21) = 18.695, p<0.001, η2=0.471).
source: and a significant linear trend (F(1,21) = 18.695, p<0.001, η2=0.471), with a more pronounced spatial saccade bias when the cue was more reliable.
evidence: Statistical test showing linear relationship between cue reliability and saccade bias.

claim: Only the 80% cue-reliability condition showed an alpha lateralization according to the location of the tested memory item that was larger following unexpected/invalid vs. expected/valid memory tests (cluster p=0.048).
source: For alpha lateralization, we found only weak spatial modulation in response to the test stimulus, with only the 80% cue-reliability condition showing a lateralization according to the location of the tested memory item that was larger following unexpected/invalid vs. expected/valid memory tests (Figure 3a, cluster p=0.048
evidence: Statistical test showing differential alpha lateralization after memory test.

claim: When the test was certain (100%), a significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed in the imperative-100% condition (cluster p=0.021).
source: When the test was certain (100%), a significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed (Figure 3b, cluster p=0.021
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias away from tested item location.

claim: When the test was certain (100%), a significant saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item was observed in the 100% condition (cluster p=0.003).
source: p=0.003, for imperative-100% and 100% conditions, respectively
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias away from tested item location.

claim: In the 80%-valid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was observed (cluster p=0.023).
source: when the nature of the test stimulus was not 100% certain (in 80/60% cue-reliability conditions), we found a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item (Figure 3b, 80%-valid block: cluster p=0.023
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias toward tested item location.

claim: In the 80%-invalid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was observed (cluster p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias toward tested item location.

claim: In the 60%-valid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was observed (cluster p=0.009).
source: 60%-valid block: cluster p=0.009
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias toward tested item location.

claim: In the 60%-invalid block, a pronounced saccade bias towards the memorized location of the tested item was observed (cluster p<0.001).
source: p<0.001, for valid-cue and invalid-cue trials, respectively
evidence: Statistical test showing saccade bias toward tested item location.

claim: There were significant clusters when comparing the saccade bias following expected (validly cued) and unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests in the 80% cue-reliability block (cluster p=0.003).
source: First, we found significant clusters when comparing the saccade bias following expected (validly cued) and unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests, in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks, as indicated by the black horizontal significance lines in Figure 3b (cluster p=0.003
evidence: Statistical comparison showing differential saccade bias between valid and invalid trials.

claim: There were significant clusters when comparing the saccade bias following expected (validly cued) and unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests in the 60% cue-reliability block (cluster p=0.025).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing differential saccade bias between valid and invalid trials.

claim: There was no statistical difference in onset latency of saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in the 80% condition (t(21) = –0.567, p=0.577, BF01=3.877 in favor of the null hypothesis).
source: For onset latency after the memory test, we found no statistical difference following expected and unexpected memory tests (80%: t(21) = –0.567, p=0.577, BF01=3.877 in favor of the null hypothesis
evidence: Statistical test and Bayesian analysis showing no difference in onset latency.

claim: There was no statistical difference in onset latency of saccade bias following expected and unexpected memory tests in the 60% condition (t(21) = –0.440, p=0.665, BF01=4.108 in favor of the null hypothesis).
source: 60%: t(21) = –0.440, p=0.665, BF01=4.108 in favor of the null hypothesis
evidence: Statistical test and Bayesian analysis showing no difference in onset latency.

claim: There was a clear difference in the offset latency of the re-orienting bias in gaze in the 80% condition (t(21) = 2.200, p=0.039).
source: In contrast, we found a clear difference in the offset latency of this re-orienting bias in gaze (80%: t(21) = 2.200, p=0.039
evidence: Statistical test showing difference in offset latency.

claim: There was a clear difference in the offset latency of the re-orienting bias in gaze in the 60% condition (t(21) = 3.409, p=0.003).
evidence: Statistical test showing difference in offset latency.

claim: There was no evidence for a significant difference in the cue-validity effect on prolonged re-orienting following memory tests between the 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks (t(21) = 0.237, p=0.815, BF01=5.962 in favor of the null hypothesis).
source: We found no evidence for a significant difference in the cue-validity effect on this prolonged re-orienting following memory tests in the 80% and 60% cue-reliability blocks (t(21) = 0.237, p=0.815, BF01=5.962 in favor of the null hypothesis).
evidence: Statistical test and Bayesian analysis showing no difference between conditions.

claim: FAL analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following the unexpected tests vs. expected tests in the 80% condition (411 ms vs. 463 ms, t(14) = 2.358, p=0.034).
source: Consistent with our jackknife-based latency analysis, the FAL analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following the unexpected tests (the invalid-cue trials) vs. expected tests (the valid-cue trials) in both 80% and 60% cue-reliability conditions (411 ms vs. 463 ms, t(14) = 2.358, p=0.034
evidence: Statistical test using FAL analysis showing prolonged saccade bias.

claim: FAL analysis revealed a significantly prolonged saccade bias following the unexpected tests vs. expected tests in the 60% condition (417 ms vs. 468 ms, t(15) = 2.168, p=0.047).
source: 417 ms vs. 468 ms, t(15) = 2.168, p=0.047; for 80% and 60% condition, respectively
evidence: Statistical test using FAL analysis showing prolonged saccade bias.

claim: There was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests in the 80% condition (346 ms vs. 374 ms, t(14) = 2.052, p=0.060).
source: Again, there was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests. (346 ms vs. 374 ms, t(14) = 2.052, p=0.060
evidence: Statistical test showing no difference in onset latency.

claim: There was no significant statistical difference in onset latency following unexpected vs. expected tests in the 60% condition (353 ms vs. 401 ms, t(15) = 1.577, p=0.136).
source: 353 ms vs. 401 ms, t(15) = 1.577, p=0.136; for 80% and 60% condition, respectively
evidence: Statistical test showing no difference in onset latency.

claim: Attention can be directed not only to external sensations but also to internal representations held in working memory.
source: Attention enables us to select and prioritize relevant information and can be directed not only to external sensations but also to internal representations held in working memory (Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Panichello and Buschman, 2021; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede and Nobre, 2023).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Studies on external attention have extensively characterized the mechanisms of both orienting of attention following predictive probabilistic cues and re-orienting of attention following unexpected perceptual targets.
source: Studies on external attention have extensively characterized the mechanisms of both orienting of attention following predictive probabilistic cues and re-orienting of attention following unexpected perceptual targets (Carrasco, 2018; Corbetta et al., 2002; Corbetta et al., 2000; Doricchi et al., 2010; Posner, 1980; Posner et al., 1982; Posner and Cohen, 1984).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Studies on internal attention have almost exclusively focused on the mechanisms supporting initial orienting following predictive retrocues.
source: In contrast, studies on internal attention – directed to representations held in working memory – have almost exclusively focused on just the former: the mechanisms supporting initial orienting following predictive retrocues (for reviews, see Myers et al., 2017; Oberauer, 2019; Sahan et al., 2020; Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede and Nobre, 2023) or temporal expectations (van Ede et al., 2017; Zokaei et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research and reviews.

claim: The brain relies on memorized locations to orient to specific objects held within the spatial layout of working memory.
source: These studies have made clear, among others, how the brain relies on memorized locations to orient to specific objects held within the spatial layout of working memory (de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2022; Günseli et al., 2019; Kuo et al., 2009; Lepsien et al., 2005; Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022; Macedo-Pascual et al., 2022; Myers et al., 2015; Poch et al., 2017; Poch et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2015; van Ede, 2018; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a; van Ede et al., 2019b; Wallis et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claim: The lateralization of 8–12 Hz posterior EEG-alpha activity is an established marker of spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
source: Building on ample prior studies, we tracked spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory using two established markers: the lateralization of 8–12 Hz posterior EEG-alpha activity (Fu et al., 2022; Günseli et al., 2019; Li et al., 2023; Macedo-Pascual et al., 2022; Myers et al., 2015; Poch et al., 2017; Poch et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2015; van Ede, 2018; van Ede et al., 2019a; Wallis et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The spatial biasing of (micro)saccades is an established marker of spatial orienting of attention within the spatial layout of visual working memory.
source: and the spatial biasing of (micro)saccades (as in de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Participants used the cue even when the cue was 80% or 60% reliable, and did so in a graded manner that depended on cue reliability.
source: Together, these results show that participants used the cue even when the cue was 80% or 60% reliable, and did so in a graded manner that depended on cue reliability.
evidence: Inference drawn from the behavioral data showing graded effects of cue reliability.

claim: The saccade bias observed during internal attentional focusing was predominantly driven by fixational micro-saccades rather than looking back to the encoded location of the memory items.
source: This further corroborates that the bias observed during internal attentional focusing was predominantly driven by fixational micro-saccades rather than looking back to the encoded location of the memory items (Johansson and Johansson, 2014; Richardson and Spivey, 2000; Spivey and Geng, 2001; Wynn et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference from data analysis with supporting citations.

claim: The saccade bias in the direction opposite from the memorized location of the tested item likely reflects 'return' saccades to the center in response to the memory test stimulus from lingering gaze-position biases following the cue.
source: This likely reflects 'return' saccades to the center in response to the memory test stimulus from lingering gaze-position biases following the cue (i.e. a residual effect from the cue-induced modulation).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: The saccade bias shows re-orienting to the mnemonic contents in mind, in response to the memory test.
source: Because the test stimulus was presented in the center, this saccade bias shows re-orienting to the mnemonic contents in mind, in response to the memory test.
evidence: Inference from the experimental design and observed data pattern.

claim: Re-orienting in mind was found not only following unexpected tests but also following expected tests.
source: Critically, we found this re-orienting in mind not only following unexpected tests (for which the preceding retrocue initially directed attention to the other, non-tested, memory item during the delay), but also following expected tests.
evidence: Direct observation from the data analysis.

claim: The spatial marker of attention re-orienting in mind after the memory test started at a similar latency after expected and unexpected memory tests.
source: While our spatial marker of attention re-orienting in mind after the memory test started at a similar latency after expected and unexpected memory tests, the marker was prolonged following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests
evidence: Direct observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The spatial marker of attention re-orienting in mind was prolonged following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests.
source: While our spatial marker of attention re-orienting in mind after the memory test started at a similar latency after expected and unexpected memory tests, the marker was prolonged following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests (Figure 3b).
evidence: Direct observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Prolonged attentional re-orienting when the test did not match the cue-induced expectation is consistent with slower responses following unexpected (invalidly cued) memory tests.
source: In contrast, we found a clear difference in the offset latency of this re-orienting bias in gaze (80%: t(21) = 2.200, p=0.039; 60%: t(21) = 3.409, p=0.003), consistent with a prolonged attentional re-orienting when the test did not match the cue-induced expectation of which memory item would likely be tested.
evidence: Inference linking the observed prolonged re-orienting to behavioral performance.

claim: Observers deploy attention to the memorized location in response to the memory test, whether or not they had already oriented their attention after the cue.
source: These results suggest that observers deploy attention to the memorized location in response to the memory test, whether or not they had already oriented their attention after the cue.
evidence: Inference from the trial-sorting analysis.

claim: Deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect an additional verification stage following expected memory tests (in valid-cue trials).
source: In other words, this suggests that deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect an additional verification stage following expected memory tests (in valid-cue trials), and a genuine re-orienting of attention to the other memory item following unexpected memory tests (in invalid-cue trials).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect a genuine re-orienting of attention to the other memory item following unexpected memory tests (in invalid-cue trials).
source: In other words, this suggests that deployment of attention after the memory test may reflect an additional verification stage following expected memory tests (in valid-cue trials), and a genuine re-orienting of attention to the other memory item following unexpected memory tests (in invalid-cue trials).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: When the cue is 100% reliable, participants may drop the other memory item.
source: When the cue is 100% reliable, participants may drop the other memory item (Astle et al., 2012; Gözenman et al., 2014; Gressmann and Janczyk, 2016; Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Gunseli et al., 2015; Oberauer, 2001; Pertzov et al., 2013; van Moorselaar et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2013)
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When the cue is 100% reliable, participants may transform the relevant item into a different format that does not invoke spatial revisiting after the memory test.
source: or transform the relevant item into a different format (cf. Larocque et al., 2014; LaRocque et al., 2013; Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2017; Rose et al., 2016; Stokes, 2015; Wolff et al., 2017) that does not invoke spatial revisiting after the memory test.
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Participants may transform the relevant item into the appropriate action plan when 100% certain.
source: For example, participants may transform the relevant item into the appropriate action plan, when 100% certain (Henderson et al., 2022; Nasrawi et al., 2023; Nasrawi and van Ede, 2022; Olivers and Roelfsema, 2020; Schneider et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019b).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When the other item cannot be dropped, the memory items likely preserve their spatial organization, inviting spatial deployment of attention following the memory test.
source: In contrast, when the other item cannot be dropped, in the case of cues that leave some uncertainty, the memory items likely preserve their spatial organization, inviting spatial deployment of attention following the memory test.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Participants may engage in a second-stage verification ('double checking') in mind, whenever cues do not predict memory tests with certainty.
source: In other words, participants may engage in a second-stage verification ('double checking') in mind, whenever cues do not predict memory tests with certainty.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: Spatial deployment (re-orienting) of attention in mind was prolonged when the test prompted a report for the memory item that was not expected to become tested, consistent with the slowing of memory-guided behavior that is typically found after unexpected memory tests.
source: Specifically, spatial deployment (re-orienting) of attention in mind was prolonged when the test prompted a report for the memory item that was not expected to become tested. This is consistent with the slowing of memory-guided behavior that is typically found after unexpected memory tests (Astle et al., 2012; Griffin and Nobre, 2003; Lepsien et al., 2005; Matsukura et al., 2007; Rerko and Oberauer, 2013; van Moorselaar et al., 2014, for reviews, see Souza and Oberauer, 2016; van Ede and Nobre, 2023), as also observed in the current study.
evidence: Inference linking observed pattern to prior literature and current behavioral data.

claim: Unexpected memory tests do not delay the process of re-orienting in mind to the appropriate memory content.
source: Thus, while unexpected memory tests do not delay the process of re-orienting in mind to the appropriate memory content, attentional deployment did become prolonged when re-focusing the unexpected memory item
evidence: Direct observation from the latency analysis.

claim: Prolonged attentional deployment following unexpected memory tests likely reflects prolonged effort to extract the relevant information from the memory item that was not expected to be tested.
source: attentional deployment did become prolonged when re-focusing the unexpected memory item, likely reflecting prolonged effort to extract the relevant information from the memory item that was not expected to be tested.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: The test stimulus was a large central stimulus that may have attenuated alpha activity, possibly making it challenging to find spatial modulations in alpha activity.
source: In our task, the test stimulus was a large central stimulus that may have attenuated alpha activity, possibly making it challenging to find spatial modulations in alpha activity (see e.g. van Ede et al., 2014), without similarly affecting gaze.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of why alpha showed weaker effects than gaze.

claim: Memory tests can invoke either a verification or a revision of our internal focus.
source: This brings attentional re-orienting to the domain of working memory and underscores how memory tests can invoke either a verification or a revision of our internal focus.
evidence: Summary inference from the overall findings.

claim: Following expected tests, internal attentional deployment was not contingent on prior orienting, suggesting an additional verification – 'double checking' – in memory.
source: Following expected tests, internal attentional deployment was not contingent on prior orienting, suggesting an additional verification – 'double checking' – in memory.
evidence: Inference from the trial-sorting analysis.

claim: Following unexpected tests, re-focusing of alternative memory content was prolonged.
source: Following unexpected tests, re-focusing of alternative memory content was prolonged.
evidence: Direct observation from the latency analysis.

claim: The study unveils a second stage of internal attentional deployment following both expected and unexpected memory tests.
source: Besides internal orienting after predictive cues, we unveil a second stage of internal attentional deployment following both expected and unexpected memory tests.
evidence: Summary of key finding from the study.

claim: The experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavior & Movement Sciences, VU University Amsterdam (reference number: VCWE-2021–009).
source: The experimental procedures were reviewed and approved by the Scientific and Ethical Review Board (VCWE) of the Faculty of Behavior & Movement Sciences, VU University Amsterdam (reference number: VCWE-2021–009).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent, and consent to publish prior to participation.
source: All participants provided written informed consent, and consent to publish prior to participation
evidence: Statement of informed consent procedures.

claim: Participants were reimbursed 10 euros per hour as compensation for their time.
source: and were reimbursed 10 euros per hour as compensation for their time.
evidence: Statement of participant compensation.

claim: Sample size was set as a multiple of 6 for counterbalancing, and was set a-priori to n=24 based on previous publications from our lab that had similar designs and focused on similar EEG and eye-tracking outcome variables.
source: Sample size was set as a multiple of 6 for counterbalancing, and was set a-priori to n=24 based on previous publications from our lab that had similar designs and focused on similar EEG and eye-tracking outcome variables (e.g. de Vries et al., 2023; Draschkow et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; van Ede et al., 2021; van Ede et al., 2020; van Ede et al., 2019a).
evidence: Statement of sample size justification with citations.
